policies.summary: Counties may adopt standards for commercial wind and solar facilities but none more restrictive than the statute, may not ban them (even temporarily) in agricultural or industrial districts, must approve compliant applications, and may not set stricter sound, height, decommissioning or property-value conditions. The law exempts projects filed before 2023-01-27, an industrial enterprise zone near the I-88/I-39 interchange (Lee-Ogle, added by P.A. 103-81) and an area in Madison County (added by P.A. 104-458).

From 2026-06-01, counties with zoning may regulate stand-alone energy storage systems only within limits set by statute: no requirements stricter than the statute or NFPA 855, no stricter sound limits than the Pollution Control Board rules, and compliant applications must be approved.

A developer of a wind, solar or storage facility of 50 MW or more in an unincorporated area may petition the Illinois Commerce Commission when a local government violates the state siting law; the Commission may issue a siting certificate if the local government denied the project, missed the statutory deadline, or never adopted a compliant ordinance, and the certificate authorizes construction.

Counties grant siting approval or special use permits for commercial wind, solar and (from 2026-06-01) energy storage facilities under state-set limits; the state has no permitting authority of its own. Since 2026-06-01 the Illinois Commerce Commission may issue a siting certificate for a facility of 50 MW or more in unincorporated areas if a local government denies or fails to act in violation of the state siting law (see IL-local_preemption-3).

Statute sets the maximum setbacks a county may require: for wind towers 2.1 times blade-tip height from nonparticipating homes and community buildings and 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines and roads, plus a 30-hour yearly shadow-flicker limit; for solar 150 feet from nonparticipating homes and 50 feet from property lines and roads, fencing of 6 to 25 feet, and panels no taller than 20 feet. Sound limits may be no stricter than state Pollution Control Board rules.

Counties regulating stand-alone energy storage must require setbacks of 150 feet from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating homes, 50 feet from their property lines and from road rights-of-way, and perimeter fencing of 7 to 25 feet; nonparticipating owners may waive the setbacks.

In September 2020, the Christian County Board voted 10-6 to approve zoning code amendments with restrictive setback and shadow flicker requirements.
restrictions.long_description: In September 2020, the Christian County Board voted 10-6 to approve zoning code amendments with restrictive setback and shadow flicker requirements. The regulations were interpreted as effectively banning wind farms in the county. Following the adoption of Public Act 102-1123 (2023), the ordinance was revised to provide that, if any of these restrictions were judicially determined to violate state law, then the limits set out in PA 102-1123 would apply.

restrictions.description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance.
restrictions.long_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning committee recommended increasing the existing 1,000-foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County Citizens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further specified that, even if neighbors agreed to waive the setback requirement, any wind tower still must be at least 1,000 feet from the nearest primary structure. In 2023, Ford County amended its zoning rules to provide that, if the existing restrictions were “judicially determined to be invalid for any reason,” then the setbacks prescribed by Public Act 102-1123 (2023) would apply.

restrictions.description: In January 2021, the Monroe County Board updated its zoning codes for wind and solar energy systems and added several restrictions for siting renewables.
restrictions.long_description: In January 2021, the Monroe County Board updated its zoning codes for wind and solar energy systems and added several restrictions for siting renewables. Among other changes, the new wind code increased setback limits to 2,640 feet from non-participating property lines; set noise limits of 30 and 35 dBA, depending on the time of day; and forbade any shadow flicker on neighboring properties and public roadways.  This ordinance is likely invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

restrictions.description: In August 2020, a moratorium on wind energy projects was extended until March 2021 with unanimous approval from the County Board.
restrictions.long_description: In August 2020, a moratorium on wind energy projects was extended until March 2021 with unanimous approval from the County Board. In January 2023, Piatt County again imposed a moratorium on applications for wind energy projects through September 2023.  This moratorium is likely invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

restrictions.description: On July 27, 2022, the Tazewell County Board voted to approve a 6-month moratorium on new wind energy projects until a new ordinance is adopted.
restrictions.long_description: On July 27, 2022, the Tazewell County Board voted to approve a 6-month moratorium on new wind energy projects until a new ordinance is adopted. The moratorium was adopted in response to a request from an organization called United Citizens of Tazewell County, LLC.  This type of moratorium would be invalid under state law pursuant to Public Act 102-1123 (2023).

projects.description: Mercer County residents have expressed opposition to a 380-acre solar farm that Birch Creek Energy has proposed for Alexis, Illinois.
projects.long_description: Mercer County residents have expressed opposition to a 380-acre solar farm that Birch Creek Energy has proposed for Alexis, Illinois. At an October 2023 meeting with the Mercer County Zoning Board, some residents expressed concerns about loss of farmland. Local opposition also focused on concerns about noise and environmental impacts, including impacts to endangered species. The Mercer County Zoning Board denied Birch Creek’s conditional use permit application in November 2023.

projects.finality_evidence: court_ruling: Alta Farms Wind Project II v. DeWitt County
projects.description: The Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt County Board despite local opposition.
projects.long_description: The Alta Wind Farm was approved in July 2020 by the DeWitt County Board despite local opposition. The 200-MW project had been proposed nearly 10 years before. In October 2020, opponents filed two separate lawsuits to stop the project but dropped both of those lawsuits in March 2021. In July 2021, the DeWitt County Board approved a motion preventing the issuance of new building permits to Enel Green Power for the Alta Wind Farm until the company could prove that its turbines could be curtailed during severe weather events. An Illinois judge then issued a mandamus order holding that the Dewitt County Board lacked legal authority to halt the issuance of building permits. The wind farm proceeded to operation in June 2023.

projects.project_name: Goose Creek Wind Project / Prosperity Wind Farm
projects.description: On February 3, 2023, the Piatt County Zoning Board of Appeals voted against recommending a zoning permit for Apex Clean Energy’s 300-MW, 50-turbine Goose Creek wind project.
projects.long_description: On February 3, 2023, the Piatt County Zoning Board of Appeals voted against recommending a zoning permit for Apex Clean Energy’s 300-MW, 50-turbine Goose Creek wind project. This followed 14 nights of hearings in November and December. Opponents of the project emphasized health issues, shadow flicker, the loss of farmland, and the lack of need for additional energy in the community. In October 2023, citing intervening changes in Illinois law, the Piatt County Board approved the project, which, by then, had been renamed Prosperity Wind Farm.

projects.description: In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy.
projects.long_description: In 2015, Clean Line Energy proposed a project to build 207 miles of a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power line between the Mississippi River and Indiana border to transmit clean energy. The Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) first approved it in 2015. Landowner and agriculture groups called Concerned Citizens and Property Owners, Illinois Agricultural Association, and Landowners Alliance of Central Illinois challenged the approval in state court, and, in 2018, an Illinois appellate court overturned the approval on the grounds that regulators improperly allowed the company to use an expedited review process. The project was eventually taken over in 2020 by Invenergy, but the previous court order still prevented the project from going forward. In 2022, Gov. J.B. Pritzker signed the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which enabled construction to proceed despite the court’s ruling. The ICC approved the project for the second time in March 2023, allowing Invenergy to start building the HVDC power line. In August 2023, an Illinois appellate court enacted a stay on implementation of the March 2023 order to decide the project’s constitutionality. In September 2023, the court lifted the stay allowing the developer to continue with planning while the appeal moves forward. In August 2024, the Illinois appellate court reversed the ICC’s March 2023 approval of the project, citing issues with the financing of the project. In November 2024, the state’s Supreme Court granted leave to hear the appeal of the appellate court’s ruling. On July 23, 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy announced the cancellation of a $4.9 billion conditional federal loan guarantee for phase one of the project from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri. In January 2026, the Illinois Supreme Court decided the pending appeal and ruled in favor of the developer, allowing the company to move forward with construction of the project.

projects.description: As of November 2022, over 1,000 people had signed a petition opposing plans for the 200-MW, 60-turbine Top Hat Wind Project over concerns about interference with radar.
projects.long_description: As of November 2022, over 1,000 people had signed a petition opposing plans for the 200-MW, 60-turbine Top Hat Wind Project over concerns about interference with radar. That same month, however, after the developers entered into an agreement with the National Weather Service to shut off the turbines in case of severe weather, the Logan County Board approved the project. Opponents, including a group called Logan County Residents Against the Top Hat Wind Factory, stated that they were considering filing a lawsuit.

projects.description: On September 10, 2024, the Will County Land Use and Development Committee voted unanimously to deny a special use permit to construct a 300-MW solar project on 3,600 acres of land in Custer and Reed townships.

The developer ACCIONA Energia presented plans for the project as early as November 2021. Local residents and officials raised concerns about visual impacts, property value impacts, loss of farmland, decommissioning.

projects.description: Soltage proposed two 5-MW solar facilities on approximately 75 acres in New Lenox Township.
projects.long_description: Soltage proposed two 5-MW solar facilities on approximately 75 acres in New Lenox Township. On May 15, 2025, the Will County Board rejected the proposal in a 16-5 vote following a petition signed by over 80 residents in opposition. The opposition cited concerns over visual impacts and possible home value decreases. Township officials also indicated that housing development plans were more economically beneficial than the proposed solar development.

projects.description: In January 2025, SunCode LLC proposed the 25.2-MW Belvidere Solar project to be located on approximately 120 acres in Caledonia Township.
projects.long_description: In January 2025, SunCode LLC proposed the 25.2-MW Belvidere Solar project to be located on approximately 120 acres in Caledonia Township. In May 2025, the Boone County Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) recommended approval of a special use permit for the project, subject to 19 conditions. In July 2025, the Boone County Administration Committee held a public meeting at which several local residents raised concerns over the project’s impact on property value, loss of agricultural land, and visual impacts. The opponents asked for stronger assurances about setbacks, screening, and decommissioning bonds before approval. The Committee recommended denial of the proposal and submitted it to the Boone County Board for a final decision. On July 31, 2025, the Board, in an 8-2 vote, approved the special use permit in accordance with the ZBA recommendation. The developer agreed to donate $50,000 to the local fire department in addition to a previous commitment of investing $100,000 to preserve local farmland.

projects.description: In 2026, SB Energy proposed the Shawnee Energy Project, a solar energy facility, to be located on private land spanning Massac and Johnson Counties.
projects.long_description: In 2026, SB Energy proposed the Shawnee Energy Project, a solar energy facility, to be located on private land spanning Massac and Johnson Counties. The Johnson County Commission granted a special use permit for that County’s portion of the project, which comprises approximately 200 MW of solar generation on 1,100 acres. In February 2026, the developer submitted an application for the special use permit to the Massac County Commission for the remaining portion of the project. On February 24, 2026, the developer hosted a public meeting at the Metropolis Elks Lodge, which was attended by the Massac County Commissioners and approximately 75 local residents. During the meeting, residents opposed to the project questioned why the meeting was not held as a formal public hearing, with a question-and-answer session. The county commissioners rescheduled the meeting. In April 2026, the Massac County Commission held a public hearing on the project at the county courthouse. Opponents of the project raised concerns about loss of farmland, excess of stormwater runoff, and questioned the lifespan of the project and decommissioning plans. The developer stated that the footprint of the Massac County portion of the project had been reduced to 650 acres and its capacity reduced from 300 MW to 150 MW. The project is estimated to produce a total of $20 million of property taxes for Massac County over the next 25 to 35 years and create 450 jobs during construction. As of June 2026, the Massac County Commission was yet to make a decision on whether to approve the project.
